title: The forgiven
hookLine: Hind, Ikrimah, Wahshi and others who fought him are forgiven when they come to him
last: WHOEVER SHUTS HIS DOOR IS SAFE.

lines: WHAT ABOUT THE ONES WHO HURT HIM?
cards: Mecca has been entered, and now comes a harder question. What happens to the people who had hurt him badly? A man who killed the Prophet's uncle.
A woman who celebrated that death. The son of a leading opponent. One by one, they come.

teach.b: Start with Wahshi. At Uhud he killed Hamza, the uncle of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps Wahshi's own account.
Later, he comes to the Prophet with a group from Ta'if, and accepts Islam. The Prophet asks: are you Wahshi? Are you the one who killed Hamza?
Wahshi says it happened as he's heard. And the Prophet accepts him, and then asks one thing: can you keep your face away from me? That detail is honest.
Forgiveness here doesn't mean the grief is gone. The door is open, and the wound is still a wound.
Then Hind, Abu Sufyan's wife, who had stood against him at Uhud.
Bukhari records what she said to him after she accepted Islam: once there was no household on earth she wanted more to see disgraced than his, and now there's none she wants more to see honored.
Then Ikrimah, son of Abu Jahl, who fled Mecca toward Yemen to escape.

teach.h: IKRIMAH: BROUGHT HOME BY HIS WIFE.
teach.b: The sirah tells that his wife, Umm Hakim, asked the Prophet for his safety, got it, and went after her husband to bring him home. He was received, not punished. Notice what these stories have in common.
None of the three earns it by being useful first.
And each one is met by a door that was already open. That doesn't erase what they did. The stories remember it plainly, right beside Hind's sentence about a household she now wanted to see honored.

how: Muslims retell the forgiveness at the conquest of Mecca from Sahih al-Bukhari and the sirah, and the stories of Wahshi, Hind and Ikrimah are told as examples of the Prophet's mercy toward former enemies.

o: former enemies received when they came to him
captives set free once a ransom was paid
Muslims who missed a march and were excused

s: forgiving Wahshi meant the Prophet acted as if nothing happened
he accepted him, and asked him to keep his face away.
Ikrimah's wife asked for his safety and brought him back
the sirah tells Umm Hakim went after him once his safety was granted.
the forgiven had to prove themselves useful first
each one simply came, and was received.

games.q: you're the Prophet. the man who killed your uncle stands in front of you and accepts Islam. what do you do?
o: accept him, and ask him to keep his face away from you.
accept him and say it never happened.
games.why: he accepted Wahshi, and asked: can you keep your face away from me? the door was open, and the grief was honest.

practice: Bring to mind one real hurt, not the biggest, one you can hold for two minutes, and remember it plainly, the way the stories remember Uhud.
Forgiving doesn't require pretending it didn't hurt; the Prophet still asked Wahshi to keep his face away, so you can keep a boundary and still picture a door left unlocked, even a crack.
If you pray, you can ask Allah to forgive them, and to forgive you.

wordCard.voice: The forgiven. Wahshi, Hind, Ikrimah and others who had fought the Prophet were accepted when they came to him, their past remembered but not held against them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: pardon, letting a wrong go; al-'Afuw, the Pardoner, is one of the names of Allah.

carryVoice: Your line: the door stayed open. A week that began under a tree ends at an open door. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3825 (Hind's words to the Prophet)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah; Malik, al-Muwatta, book of marriage (Ikrimah and Umm Hakim)
